escenas.titulo: Who has a stake in a business?

visual.pie: Internal and external stakeholders, and the conflicts between them

turnos.t: Welcome to part three, the last three boxes of your Unit one poster: stakeholders, growth and evolution, and multinational companies.
Picture a business that wants to expand its factory.
Shareholders are happy, because profit may rise.
Workers ask if their jobs are safe.
Neighbours worry about noise and lorries.
Everyone wants something different.
Here is the definition: a stakeholder is an individual or group with an interest in a business, because they affect it or are affected by its activities.
And the classic trap.
A shareholder owns shares in a company, so shareholders are just one type of stakeholder.
Every shareholder is a stakeholder, but not every stakeholder is a shareholder.

escenas.titulo: Internal stakeholders and what they want

tarjetas.detalle: Pay, benefits, job security, working conditions
Set and meet objectives; career, bonuses, job security
Return: dividends and capital gains (a rising share price)

turnos.t: Internal stakeholders are part of the organization, directly involved in its decisions.
There are three groups.
Employees want pay, benefits, job security and good working conditions.
Managers set the objectives and make sure they are met, but they also want a career, bonuses and security.
Shareholders own the company and want a return: dividends, and capital gains, which means a rising share price.
Some books call shareholders external, because in big public companies they don't run the business day to day.
But they appoint the board of directors, which chooses the chief executive, so most sources call them internal.
Roles also overlap: in June twenty twenty, Zoom paid its employees stock bonuses, so they became shareholders too.

visual.titulo: External stakeholders and their main interests
filas: Regular orders, paid fairly and on time
Loans repaid on time with interest

turnos.t: External stakeholders are outside the organization, but they affect it or are affected by it.
Customers want quality, safety, a fair price and good service.
Suppliers want regular orders and to be paid on time.
The government wants taxes, jobs and firms that obey the law.
The local community wants jobs, but also low pollution and safe roads.
Pressure groups fight for their cause, like the environment.
Banks want their loans repaid with interest.
Trade unions defend employees' pay and rights.
Even competitors count.
Exam tip: to explain any reaction, start from what that group wants.
For a two-mark distinguish question: internal means part of the organization, like employees; external means outside but affected, like suppliers.

filas: Lower tax bill vs fair taxes

turnos.t: Why do stakeholders clash?
Because resources are limited and objectives differ.
Money paid in wages cannot also be paid in dividends.
So every decision creates winners and losers.
Stakeholder conflict is a situation in which the interests of different stakeholder groups cannot all be met by the same business decision.
But there is also alignment: most stakeholders are better off if the business thrives, and interests are usually more aligned in the long term than in the short term.
In a four-mark explain question, give each group's interest, then the mechanism.
Employees want higher wages.
Higher wages raise costs, so profit falls, so shareholders receive smaller dividends.
That mechanism is where the marks are.

tarjetas.detalle: High power, high interest: shareholders, farmers' union
High power, lower interest: regional government
High interest, less power: job-seekers, environmental group
Low power, low interest: distant customers

turnos.t: Now an invented case from the app: VoltNord wants to build a battery factory near Lleida.
Four hundred jobs and local taxes, but it would take river water that farmers need in a drought.
Job-seekers support it; farmers and an environmental group oppose it.
Shareholders want to start this year, and the regional government wants the jobs but worries about water.
To organise this, use a stakeholder map.
It classifies stakeholders by power and interest, to decide how closely to manage each group.
High power and high interest: manage closely.
High power, lower interest: keep satisfied.
High interest, less power: keep informed.
Low and low: monitor.
And a map is a snapshot: a farmers' union with media coverage gains power.

escenas.titulo: Nissan in Barcelona: change brings conflict

puntos.texto: Nissan announces it will close its Barcelona plants
Workers strike; production stops for about four months
Deal with workers: closure delayed to December 2021
Last vehicles made at the Zona Franca plant

turnos.t: The syllabus asks why change can bring conflict among stakeholders.
Because change redistributes costs and benefits.
Shareholders may gain from lower costs, while employees lose jobs, suppliers lose orders and the community loses income.
A real case: on the twenty-eighth of May, twenty twenty, Nissan announced it would close its Barcelona plants, with close to three thousand direct jobs at stake, although estimates vary.
Workers went on strike, and production stopped for about four months.
In August, a deal delayed the closure to December twenty twenty-one, when the last vehicles left the Zona Franca plant.
That deal is negotiation and compromise.
A balanced judgement: it ended the strike and gave people time, but it did not save the jobs.

visual.nota: Win-win at VoltNord: recycle water + train and hire local people

turnos.t: So how does a business reduce conflict?
Identify the stakeholders and their interests.
Map their power and interest.
Communicate early and honestly, and consult, which means listening before deciding.
Negotiate a compromise, like Nissan's delay.
Then monitor, because power changes.
Look for win-win options: if VoltNord recycles its water and trains local people, farmers keep their water and villagers get jobs.
When nobody can be fully satisfied, managers must choose whose interests come first, and justify it with the mission and objectives.
And outsiders can force change: in twenty twenty-one, Dutch environmental groups won a court case ordering Shell to cut its carbon dioxide emissions by forty-five per cent by twenty thirty.

escenas.titulo: Economies of scale and average cost

visual.pie: Economies and diseconomies of scale, internal and external growth, reasons to grow or stay small

turnos.t: Next box on the poster: growth and evolution.
Economies and diseconomies of scale, internal and external growth, and reasons to grow or stay small.
It all starts with average cost, which is total cost divided by output.
One thousand units for fifty thousand euros: fifty euros each.
Four thousand units for one hundred and sixty thousand euros: forty euros each, a twenty per cent fall.
Lower average cost means lower prices, or more profit at the same price.
Definition: economies of scale are the cost advantages a business gains as its scale of production increases, leading to a lower average cost per unit.
The main reason: fixed costs are spread over more units.

visual.titulo: Average cost per unit as output grows (illustrative)

turnos.t: These bars use the app's illustrative numbers.
Fifty euros at one thousand units, forty-four at two thousand, forty at four thousand, and thirty-eight at six thousand: the lowest point.
Then it rises: forty at eight thousand, forty-five at ten thousand.
That is the U-shaped curve.
On the way down, economies of scale.
After the bottom, diseconomies of scale: the rise in average cost per unit that occurs when a business grows beyond its most efficient size.
That lowest point is often called the minimum efficient scale; here, six thousand units.
If you draw it, put output on the horizontal axis, average cost on the vertical, and label where economies end and diseconomies begin.

escenas.titulo: Internal economies of scale: six types

filas: Lower interest: banks see less risk
Advert cost spread over more sales

turnos.t: Internal economies of scale come from the firm's own growth.
There are six types.
Purchasing: a chain buys coffee by the tonne and gets bulk discounts.
Technical: bigger, more efficient machines, like an automated bakery line.
Financial: banks see big firms as less risky, so they charge lower interest.
Managerial: specialist managers, like a dedicated finance director.
Marketing: one national advert costs the same with one hundred stores or one thousand, so the cost per unit sold falls.
Risk-bearing: many products and markets, so a fall in one is offset elsewhere.
In a four-mark question, bulk buying alone is one mark.
The second mark is the mechanism: discounts, so the material cost per unit falls.

escenas.titulo: Diseconomies, and effects beyond the firm

tarjetas.detalle: The firm grows: bulk buying, technology, cheaper finance
Too big: slow communication, poor coordination, low motivation
The industry or area grows: suppliers, trained workers, transport
The area grows too much: congestion, higher rents and wages

turnos.t: Now the downside of size.
Internal diseconomies appear when a firm gets too big.
Communication: messages pass through many layers and get distorted.
Coordination: departments and countries pull in different directions.
Motivation: staff feel like a number, absenteeism rises and productivity falls.
External effects hit every firm in an industry or area.
External economies come from the growth of the whole industry or area: specialist suppliers nearby, trained workers, transport links.
That's why parts suppliers cluster around the Seat plant in Martorell.
External diseconomies come when an area grows too much: traffic congestion delays deliveries, and rents and wages rise.
So remember four boxes: internal or external, economy or diseconomy.
